newsitem.title: USA: U.S. crop insurance covers pet care and golfing.
newsitem.headline: U.S. crop insurance covers pet care and golfing.

text.p: Taxpayers paid tens of thousands of dollars for insurance agents' golf outings, a baseball skybox, pet care and a Canadian fishing vacation as part of the federal crop insurance programme that is facing a budget crisis, U.S. investigators said Thursday.
Those expenses plus administrative costs and miscellaneous fees added up to $43 million in overcharges in 1994 and 1995 by the insurance companies, the General Accounting Office said in a new report.
The congressional investigators described example after example of "excessive" payments to private insurance agents by the Agriculture Department's Federal Crop Insurance Corporation.

The corporation is a federally-funded safety net for farmers against losses from floods, hurricanes, droughts and other natural disasters. It offers catastrophic insurance for a flat $50 processing fee, and sells "buy-up" insurance to cover smaller losses for a premium paid by the farmer.
The federal crop insurance corporation conducts the programme mainly through private insurance companies, and reimburses the companies for expenses in selling the policies.

The federal crop insurance programme is facing a budget crisis, with $200 million extra needed to fund fiscal 1998 sales commissions of insurance agents, said Indiana Sen. Richard Lugar, chairman of the Senate Agriculture Committee.

Last year, the federal government spent a record $1.76 billion on the crop insurance programme, triple the annual amount spent a decade ago. Taxpayers paid $2.50 for every $1 paid by farmers, for a subsidy rate of about 60 percent, Sen. Lugar said.

"It is fair to ask whether it is necessary to provide large subsidies for revenue insurance permanently," Lugar said. "Market-based commercial reinsurance could be developed based on exchange-traded futures and options contracts."

One of the nine insurance companies audited by GAO investigators sent managers to a three-day meeting at a resort and billed the government for luxury rooms at $323 per night, $405 in golf green fees, $139 in charges at a golf pro shop and other expenses, according to Robert Robinson, director of food and agriculture issues for the GAO.
The following year, the same company billed the government nearly $50,000 to pay for a company retreat at the same exclusive resort.

Other insurance companies spent $44,000 for a Canadian fishing trip for a group of agents, $18,000 to rent and furnish a baseball stadium sky box, and $22,000 for a trip to Las Vegas for company employees, Robinson said.
One insurance firm paid for tickets to an amusement park, spouse travel and pet care, then claimed reimbursement as crop insurance delivery expenses, he added.

"While a number of the companies believe that the type of expenses described above are important to maintaining an effective sales force and supporting their companies' mission, we, along with the FCIC, believe that most of these expenses appear to be excessive," Robinson said in testimony Thursday before a Senate Agriculture subcommittee.
Insurance industry officials criticised the GAO report, saying the reimbursed expenses had no impact on farmers.
